name: Psychology
areas: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Psychology Study Design, Units 3 and 4. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs, not VCAA syllabus numbering.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Use class resources and past examinations for official practice.
papers: Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.title: Aims, hypotheses, variables and operationalisation
points.detail: Writing an aim and a hypothesis that names the population, the independent and dependent variables and the predicted direction; operationalising variables so they can be measured.

questions.q: A researcher investigates whether sleep deprivation affects reaction time in adolescents. Write an operationalised hypothesis and identify the variables.
answer: Hypothesis: adolescents aged 15 to 18 who are restricted to four hours of sleep will have slower mean reaction times on a computerised task than those who sleep eight hours.
Independent variable: hours of sleep, operationalised as four hours versus eight hours.
Dependent variable: reaction time, operationalised as mean milliseconds taken to respond on the task.
An operationalised hypothesis states the population, both variables in measurable terms and the expected direction.

points.title: Extraneous and confounding variables
points.detail: The difference between a variable that may affect results and one that has systematically affected them; participant, situational, order and experimenter effects.

questions.q: Distinguish between an extraneous and a confounding variable, and give an example of a confounding variable in a memory experiment.
answer: An extraneous variable is any variable other than the independent variable that may affect the dependent variable.
A confounding variable is one that has systematically varied with the independent variable and has therefore affected the results, so an alternative explanation exists.
For example, if the group given the mnemonic technique was also tested in a quiet room while the control group was tested in a noisy one, noise level is a confounding variable.

points.title: Population, sample and sampling techniques
points.detail: Random, stratified and convenience sampling; the representativeness of each and the effect on the ability to generalise findings to the population.

questions.q: Explain why stratified sampling may produce a more representative sample than convenience sampling, and describe how it is carried out.
answer: The population is divided into strata such as age groups or year levels, and participants are selected from each stratum in the same proportion as in the population.
This ensures each subgroup is represented in the sample in proportion to its presence in the population.
Convenience sampling selects whoever is easily available, which may over-represent one subgroup, so findings generalise less well.

points.title: Experimental research designs
points.detail: Within subjects, between subjects and mixed designs; the advantages and limitations of each, including order effects and participant differences.

questions.q: Compare a within subjects and a between subjects design, stating one advantage and one limitation of each.
answer: In a within subjects design each participant completes every condition, which eliminates individual participant differences between conditions and needs fewer participants.
However, it is vulnerable to order effects such as practice or fatigue, which can be reduced by counterbalancing.
In a between subjects design different participants are allocated to each condition, avoiding order effects, but participant differences may confound the results unless allocation is random.

points.title: Controls, placebos and blind procedures
points.detail: The role of a control group, the placebo effect, and single-blind and double-blind procedures in reducing participant and experimenter expectancy effects.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of a double-blind procedure and identify the effect it controls for that a single-blind procedure does not.
answer: In a double-blind procedure neither the participants nor the researcher interacting with them knows the allocation to conditions.
A single-blind procedure controls the placebo effect by keeping participants unaware of their condition.
A double-blind procedure additionally controls the experimenter effect, where a researcher's expectations unintentionally influence participant behaviour or the recording of results.

points.title: Descriptive statistics and interpreting results
points.detail: Mean, median, mode, standard deviation and percentage change; describing what a difference between group means shows and its limitations.

questions.q: Two groups have the same mean score but very different standard deviations. Explain what this indicates about the results.
answer: The average performance of the two groups was the same.
The group with the larger standard deviation had scores that were more widely spread around the mean, indicating greater variability between participants.
The group with the smaller standard deviation performed more consistently, so the mean is a more typical representation of its participants.

points.title: Statistical significance and conclusions
points.detail: The meaning of p less than 0.05, the difference between statistical significance and practical importance, and the wording of a conclusion that is limited to the sample and variables tested.

questions.q: A study reports a result with p equal to 0.03. Explain what this means and state one thing it does not mean.
answer: There is a 3 per cent probability that a difference this large would occur due to chance alone, so the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level.
The researcher can conclude that the difference is unlikely to be due to chance and may be attributed to the independent variable, provided the study was well controlled.
It does not mean the effect is large or practically important, and it does not prove the hypothesis.

points.title: Informed consent and voluntary participation
points.detail: Providing participants with a full written description of the study before agreeing, obtaining consent from a guardian where required, and ensuring participation is free from coercion.

questions.q: Explain the difference between informed consent procedures and voluntary participation, and state what is required when participants are under 18.
answer: Informed consent procedures require that participants are given a written statement of the purpose, procedures and risks and indicate their understanding before agreeing.
Voluntary participation requires that the decision to take part is made freely, without pressure, coercion or inducement.
Participants under 18 require the informed consent of a parent or guardian in addition to their own assent.

points.title: Withdrawal rights, confidentiality and anonymity
points.detail: The right to discontinue at any time without penalty and to have data removed; the obligation to protect participants' personal information and to report results without identifying individuals.

questions.q: Explain how a researcher upholds confidentiality when publishing the results of a study.
answer: Personal information is stored securely and is not disclosed to anyone outside the research team.
Results are reported as group data, or individuals are identified only by code, so no participant can be recognised.
Data must also be disposed of securely once the study is complete.

points.title: Deception and debriefing
points.detail: When deception may be justified, the requirement to debrief participants fully at the conclusion of the study and to provide support and counselling where needed.

questions.q: A study requires participants to be misled about its true purpose. Explain when this is acceptable and what must follow.
answer: Deception is only acceptable when knowing the true purpose would change the participants' behaviour and invalidate the results, and when it causes no lasting harm.
Participants must be fully debriefed at the conclusion of the study, including the true purpose and the reason deception was used.
They must be given the opportunity to withdraw their data and offered support or counselling if any distress resulted.

points.title: Ethical concepts
points.detail: Beneficence, integrity, justice, non-maleficence and respect, and how each is applied when planning and reporting psychological research.

questions.q: Identify the ethical concept breached in each case: a researcher publishes only the results supporting their hypothesis; a study recruits participants only from one wealthy school but claims to describe all adolescents.
answer: Publishing only supportive results breaches integrity, which requires the honest reporting of all findings regardless of outcome.
Recruiting from only one privileged group and generalising breaches justice, which requires fair consideration and distribution of the benefits and burdens of research.
Both also undermine respect for participants and the community who rely on the research being accurate.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Divisions of the nervous system
points.detail: The central and peripheral nervous systems, the somatic and autonomic divisions, and the sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric branches of the autonomic nervous system.

questions.q: A person is startled by a loud noise. Name the nervous system divisions involved in the resulting increase in heart rate, from the brain outwards.
answer: The central nervous system processes the stimulus and initiates the response.
The message travels via the peripheral nervous system, specifically the autonomic division, which controls visceral muscles and organs.
Within the autonomic division the sympathetic nervous system is activated, increasing heart rate to prepare the body for action.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Conscious and unconscious responses
points.detail: Voluntary responses controlled by the somatic nervous system and involuntary responses controlled by the autonomic nervous system, with examples of each.

questions.q: Distinguish between a conscious and an unconscious response to a stimulus, giving one example of each.
answer: A conscious response is voluntary and involves awareness and intentional control, such as deciding to pick up a pen, and is carried out by the somatic nervous system.
An unconscious response is involuntary and occurs without awareness or intention, such as pupil constriction in bright light, and is carried out by the autonomic nervous system.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: The spinal reflex
points.detail: The unconscious, adaptive reflex arc initiated by the spinal cord, and the order of sensory neuron, interneuron and motor neuron before the brain registers the stimulus.

questions.q: Explain the role of the spinal cord in a spinal reflex and why this response is adaptive.
answer: Sensory neurons carry the message to the spinal cord, where an interneuron transfers it directly to a motor neuron that produces the movement.
The spinal cord initiates the response before the message reaches the brain, so the movement occurs without conscious awareness.
This is adaptive because the reduced time taken means the body withdraws from a harmful stimulus more quickly, limiting injury.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Neurons and neural transmission
points.detail: Sensory, motor and interneurons; dendrites, axon, myelin, axon terminals and the synaptic gap; the lock-and-key process of transmission across the synapse.

questions.q: Describe how a message is transmitted from one neuron to the next across the synapse.
answer: The action potential travels down the axon to the axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron.
Neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic gap from vesicles in the terminal buttons.
The neurotransmitter binds to receptor sites on the dendrites of the postsynaptic neuron in a lock-and-key process, producing an excitatory or inhibitory effect.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters
points.detail: Glutamate as the main excitatory neurotransmitter and GABA as the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, and the consequences of an imbalance between them.

questions.q: Compare the effects of glutamate and GABA on postsynaptic neurons and state one consequence of low GABA activity.
answer: Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter and increases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire.
GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter and decreases the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will fire, calming neural activity.
Low GABA activity leaves the nervous system over-excited, which is associated with heightened anxiety and is one biological contributor to specific phobia.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Neuromodulators
points.detail: Dopamine and serotonin as neuromodulators that influence the activity of many neurons over a wider area, and their roles in reward, motivation and mood.

questions.q: Distinguish between a neurotransmitter and a neuromodulator, and state the role of dopamine.
answer: A neurotransmitter acts on the adjacent postsynaptic neuron and has a rapid, localised effect.
A neuromodulator affects a larger number of neurons over a wider region and alters how they respond to other neurotransmitters, with slower and longer lasting effects.
Dopamine is associated with reward-based learning, motivation and voluntary movement, and is released when a behaviour produces a rewarding outcome.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Synaptic plasticity
points.detail: Long-term potentiation and long-term depression, and the structural changes of sprouting, rerouting and pruning that underlie learning and memory.

questions.q: Explain long-term potentiation and its role in learning.
answer: Long-term potentiation is the long-lasting strengthening of a synaptic connection that results from repeated, high-frequency stimulation.
The postsynaptic neuron becomes more responsive, with more receptor sites and stronger signals, so less stimulation is needed to activate it.
This strengthening of neural pathways is the physical basis of learning and the formation of long-term memory.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Stress as a psychobiological process
points.detail: Stress, stressors, eustress and distress; acute and chronic stress; the physiological and psychological features of the stress response.

questions.q: Distinguish between eustress and distress and explain why the same stressor can produce either.
answer: Eustress is a positive psychological response to a stressor, involving feelings of excitement and enthusiasm alongside physiological arousal.
Distress is a negative psychological response involving anxiety, dread or anger, with similar physiological arousal.
Whether a stressor produces eustress or distress depends on the individual's appraisal of it, so the same event may be motivating for one person and threatening for another.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: The fight-flight-freeze response
points.detail: Sympathetic activation and the role of adrenaline in mobilising energy; the freeze response as a parasympathetic-dominant immobilisation; the return to homeostasis.

questions.q: Describe three physiological changes produced by the fight-flight-freeze response and explain how each supports survival.
answer: Heart rate and blood pressure increase, delivering more oxygen and glucose to the skeletal muscles for action.
Pupils dilate, allowing more light to enter and improving detection of the threat.
Digestion slows and blood is redirected from the digestive system to the muscles, conserving energy for immediate physical action.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Cortisol and chronic stress
points.detail: The role of cortisol in sustaining energy during prolonged stress, and the effects of persistently elevated cortisol on immune function and health.

questions.q: Explain the role of cortisol during prolonged stress and one negative consequence of chronically elevated levels.
answer: Cortisol is released more slowly than adrenaline and maintains elevated blood glucose, providing sustained energy during an extended stressor.
It also temporarily suppresses non-essential functions, including aspects of the immune response and inflammation.
Chronically elevated cortisol leaves the immune system suppressed, so the person becomes more vulnerable to illness and infection.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: The gut-brain axis
points.detail: The bidirectional communication between the enteric nervous system and the central nervous system, the role of the vagus nerve and gut microbiota, and the influence on stress and mood.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the gut-brain axis and give one example of communication in each direction.
answer: The gut-brain axis is the bidirectional link between the enteric nervous system of the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system, largely via the vagus nerve.
From brain to gut: psychological stress can slow digestion and produce nausea or discomfort.
From gut to brain: the gut microbiota produce chemicals that influence neurotransmitter activity and can affect mood and stress responses.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
points.detail: The alarm reaction with shock and countershock, the resistance stage and the exhaustion stage; the pattern of resistance to stress across the three stages.

questions.q: Describe the three stages of the General Adaptation Syndrome and what happens to the body's resistance in each.
answer: Alarm reaction: in shock, resistance drops below normal as the body reacts as though injured; in countershock, sympathetic activation raises resistance above normal.
Resistance: the body maintains a high level of resistance to the stressor, with cortisol sustaining arousal, but resistance to other stressors falls.
Exhaustion: resources are depleted, resistance drops below normal and the person becomes vulnerable to illness, extreme fatigue and physical damage.
The model is biological and does not account for individual psychological differences in appraisal.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Lazarus and Folkman's Transactional Model
points.detail: Primary appraisal of an event as irrelevant, benign-positive or stressful, secondary appraisal of coping resources, and the continual reappraisal of both.

questions.q: Use the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping to explain why two students respond differently to the same examination.
answer: In primary appraisal each student judges the significance of the examination; one may judge it as a threat while the other judges it as a challenge.
In secondary appraisal each evaluates the coping resources available to them, such as preparation, time and support.
A student who appraises the event as a threat and their resources as inadequate experiences stress.
The model explains individual differences because the appraisal, not the event itself, determines the stress response, and appraisals can be revised.

points.area: Unit 3 AoS 1 — The nervous system and stress
points.title: Coping strategies and coping flexibility
points.detail: Approach and avoidance strategies, context-specific effectiveness, and coping flexibility as the ability to adjust strategies to changing demands.

questions.q: Distinguish between approach and avoidance coping strategies and explain what is meant by context-specific effectiveness.
answer: Approach strategies confront the stressor directly, such as making a study plan or seeking information.
Avoidance strategies evade or deny the stressor, such as distraction or withdrawal, which may reduce distress briefly but usually does not resolve the problem.

Context-specific effectiveness means a coping strategy is only effective when it matches the demands of the particular stressor; avoidance may be appropriate for an uncontrollable stressor but not a controllable one.

points.title: Classical conditioning
points.detail: The three-phase process of before, during and after conditioning, and the roles of the neutral stimulus, unconditioned stimulus and response, and conditioned stimulus and response.

questions.q: A dog begins to salivate at the sound of a can opener. Identify the neutral stimulus, unconditioned stimulus, unconditioned response, conditioned stimulus and conditioned response.
answer: Neutral stimulus: the sound of the can opener before conditioning, which produced no salivation.
Unconditioned stimulus: the food; unconditioned response: salivation to the food.
Conditioned stimulus: the sound of the can opener after repeated pairing with food.
Conditioned response: salivation to the sound alone.

points.title: Operant conditioning
points.detail: The three-phase model of antecedent, behaviour and consequence; positive and negative reinforcement and punishment, and the effect of each on the likelihood of the behaviour.

questions.q: Classify each consequence and state its effect: a student is excused from homework for finishing early; a student loses phone privileges for lateness.
answer: Being excused from homework removes an unpleasant stimulus, so this is negative reinforcement.
Negative reinforcement increases the likelihood that the student will finish early again.
Losing phone privileges removes a desirable stimulus, so this is negative punishment, sometimes called response cost.
Negative punishment decreases the likelihood of the lateness recurring.

points.title: Comparing classical and operant conditioning
points.detail: The role of the learner as passive or active, the timing of the stimulus relative to the response, and the voluntary or involuntary nature of the behaviour.

questions.q: State three differences between classical and operant conditioning.
answer: In classical conditioning the learner is passive, while in operant conditioning the learner is active and operates on the environment.
In classical conditioning the response is reflexive and involuntary, while in operant conditioning the behaviour is voluntary.
In classical conditioning the stimulus precedes the response, while in operant conditioning the consequence follows the behaviour and determines its future frequency.

points.title: Observational learning
points.detail: Bandura's five stages of attention, retention, reproduction, motivation and reinforcement, and the role of vicarious reinforcement and punishment.

questions.q: A child watches an older sibling being praised for helping and later helps without being asked. Explain this using the stages of observational learning.
answer: Attention: the child actively watched and focused on the sibling's behaviour.
Retention: the child formed and stored a mental representation of the behaviour.
Reproduction: the child had the physical and cognitive ability to carry out the behaviour.
Motivation and reinforcement: seeing the sibling praised provided vicarious reinforcement, motivating the child to reproduce the behaviour and receive reinforcement themselves.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing
points.detail: Multimodal, place-based learning embedded in Country and kinship; story sharing, songlines, symbols and images, non-verbal learning and community links as ways knowledge is transmitted.

questions.q: Describe two features of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing and explain how they differ from a Western classroom approach.
answer: Learning is multimodal and patterned, using story sharing, song, dance, symbols and images together rather than a single channel such as written text.
Knowledge is embedded in Country and in relationships, so where learning occurs and who is present are part of the knowledge itself.
This differs from a Western classroom model in which knowledge is often abstracted from place and transmitted verbally or in writing by an individual teacher.

points.title: Songlines and sung narratives
points.detail: Songlines as a place-based method of encoding and retrieving large amounts of information across generations, linking route, story, song and Country.

questions.q: Explain how songlines function as a memory system and why they are effective.
answer: A songline links information to a sequence of locations along a route, so the physical landscape provides an ordered set of retrieval cues.
The information is encoded in narrative and song, which add rhythm, rhyme and meaning that aid retention.
Because the knowledge is tied to Country and repeatedly performed within a community, it can be preserved accurately across many generations.

points.title: The Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model
points.detail: Sensory, short-term and long-term memory stores, and their differences in capacity, duration and function; the processes of attention, encoding, rehearsal and retrieval.

questions.q: Describe the capacity and duration of each store in the Atkinson-Shiffrin model and the process needed to move information between them.
answer: Sensory memory has an unlimited capacity and a duration of up to about 4 seconds for iconic and echoic memory.
Short-term memory holds about 5 to 9 items for about 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal.
Long-term memory has a potentially unlimited capacity and duration.
Attention moves information from sensory to short-term memory, and rehearsal, particularly elaborative rehearsal, moves it to long-term memory.

points.title: Explicit and implicit memory
points.detail: Episodic and semantic memory as consciously retrieved explicit memories; procedural and classically conditioned memories as implicit memories retrieved without conscious awareness.

questions.q: Classify each as explicit or implicit and name the subtype: remembering your first day of school; riding a bicycle; knowing the capital of France.
answer: Remembering your first day of school is an explicit episodic memory, because it is a personally experienced event retrieved consciously.
Riding a bicycle is an implicit procedural memory, retrieved and performed without conscious awareness of the steps.
Knowing the capital of France is an explicit semantic memory, consisting of general factual knowledge.

points.title: Brain regions involved in memory
points.detail: The roles of the hippocampus, amygdala, neocortex, basal ganglia and cerebellum in encoding, consolidating and storing different types of memory.

questions.q: Name the brain region primarily responsible for each and state its role: forming new explicit memories; emotional memory; implicit procedural memory.
answer: The hippocampus encodes and consolidates new explicit memories before they are stored in the neocortex.
The amygdala encodes the emotional component of memories, which strengthens consolidation of emotionally significant events.
The cerebellum encodes implicit procedural memories, particularly those involving fine motor skills and classically conditioned reflexes.
The basal ganglia also contribute to implicit procedural memories involving habits and voluntary movement.

points.title: Autobiographical memory and imagining the future
points.detail: The reconstruction of episodic and semantic memory when recalling the past and when imagining possible futures, and the shared neural basis of both processes.

questions.q: Explain why damage to the hippocampus can impair a person's ability to imagine future events, not only to recall past ones.
answer: Imagining a possible future involves combining episodic details and semantic knowledge into a coherent scene, which is the same constructive process used in recall.
The hippocampus is central to combining these elements into an integrated representation.
Damage therefore impairs both the reconstruction of past episodes and the construction of imagined future ones.

points.title: Alzheimer's disease
points.detail: The role of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in progressive neuron death, the resulting anterograde and then retrograde amnesia, and the effect on daily functioning.

questions.q: Describe the neurological changes in Alzheimer's disease and their effect on memory.
answer: Amyloid plaques form outside the neurons and neurofibrillary tangles form inside them, disrupting communication and causing neuron death.
Damage begins in the hippocampus, so the earliest effect is anterograde amnesia, an inability to form new explicit memories.
As the damage spreads through the neocortex, previously stored memories are also lost, producing retrograde amnesia and a decline in language and reasoning.

points.title: Aphantasia
points.detail: The inability to generate voluntary mental imagery, its effect on the recall of visual detail and on imagining the future, and the fact that semantic knowledge remains intact.

questions.q: Explain how aphantasia affects a person's ability to recall an event and to imagine a future event.
answer: A person with aphantasia cannot generate voluntary mental images, so recall of an event lacks visual detail and is drawn on factual knowledge instead.
Imagining a future event is similarly affected, because the visual construction of the scene is not available.
Semantic knowledge of what happened, or of what a future event would involve, remains intact.

points.title: Written mnemonics
points.detail: Acronyms, acrostics and the method of loci, and how each improves encoding and retrieval by adding organisation, meaning or spatial cues.

questions.q: Explain how the method of loci improves recall and state one situation in which it is particularly useful.
answer: Information to be remembered is associated with a sequence of familiar physical locations along a route.
Mentally moving through the route at retrieval provides an ordered set of cues, each linked to one item.
It is particularly useful for recalling lists of items in a fixed order, because the order of the locations preserves the sequence.

points.title: Consciousness as a continuum
points.detail: Normal waking consciousness and altered states of consciousness, and the variation of awareness, controlled and automatic processing, perception of time and emotional awareness along the continuum.

questions.q: Describe three characteristics that differ between normal waking consciousness and an altered state of consciousness.
answer: Awareness of surroundings and of internal states is reduced in an altered state compared with normal waking consciousness.
Controlled processing is impaired, so tasks requiring attention and effort are performed less accurately.
Perception of time becomes distorted, and emotional awareness and self-control may be heightened or blunted.

points.title: Measuring sleep
points.detail: Objective measures using electroencephalography, electro-oculography and electromyography, and subjective measures including sleep diaries and video monitoring.

questions.q: Name the three physiological devices used in a sleep laboratory and state what each measures.
answer: An electroencephalograph detects and records the electrical activity of the brain, identifying the frequency and amplitude of brain waves.
An electro-oculograph records eye movement, which distinguishes REM sleep from NREM sleep.
An electromyograph records the electrical activity of muscles, showing the muscle atonia characteristic of REM sleep.

points.title: NREM and REM sleep
points.detail: The characteristics of NREM stages and REM sleep, including brain wave patterns, muscle activity, eye movement and dreaming, and the cycling through stages across the night.

questions.q: Compare REM sleep and NREM stage 3 sleep on brain wave activity, muscle tone and the proportion of the night in which each predominates.
answer: REM sleep shows high-frequency, low-amplitude brain waves similar to those of waking, while NREM stage 3 shows low-frequency, high-amplitude delta waves.
REM sleep involves muscle atonia so the body is effectively paralysed, while muscle tone is present in NREM sleep.
NREM stage 3 predominates in the first half of the night, and REM periods lengthen and predominate towards the morning.

points.title: Circadian and ultradian rhythms
points.detail: The approximately 24 hour sleep-wake cycle as a circadian rhythm and the roughly 90 minute cycle of sleep stages as an ultradian rhythm.

questions.q: Distinguish between a circadian and an ultradian rhythm, using sleep as an example of each.
answer: A circadian rhythm has a cycle of about 24 hours, such as the sleep-wake cycle governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
An ultradian rhythm has a cycle shorter than 24 hours, such as the roughly 90 minute cycle through NREM and REM sleep stages that repeats four to five times per night.

points.title: Sleep across the lifespan
points.detail: Changes in total sleep duration and in the proportion of REM and NREM sleep from infancy through adolescence to late adulthood, and the reasons for these changes.

questions.q: Describe how the amount and composition of sleep change from infancy to late adulthood.
answer: Newborns sleep around 16 hours per day with about half of that in REM sleep, supporting rapid brain development.
Total sleep time decreases across childhood and adolescence, with adolescents requiring around 8 to 10 hours, and the proportion of REM sleep falls to about 20 to 25 per cent.
Older adults sleep for a similar or slightly reduced total time but obtain much less NREM stage 3 sleep and wake more frequently during the night.

points.title: Adolescent sleep-wake shift
points.detail: The delayed release of melatonin in adolescence producing later sleep onset and offset, and the conflict between this shift and early school start times.

questions.q: Explain the adolescent sleep-wake shift and why it often results in partial sleep deprivation.
answer: During adolescence melatonin is released about one to two hours later than in childhood, so the adolescent does not feel sleepy until later at night.
The natural waking time also shifts later, but school start times remain early.
The adolescent therefore obtains fewer hours of sleep than the 8 to 10 required, accumulating a sleep debt across the school week.

points.title: Zeitgebers
points.detail: External cues that entrain the sleep-wake cycle, including light and blue light in particular, temperature and eating and drinking patterns.

questions.q: Explain how exposure to blue light from a screen at night affects the sleep-wake cycle.
answer: Light is the primary zeitgeber, detected by the eyes and relayed to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, which regulates melatonin release by the pineal gland.
Blue light suppresses melatonin release because it mimics daylight.
Sleep onset is therefore delayed, shifting the circadian rhythm later and reducing total sleep time if waking time is fixed.

points.title: Effects of partial sleep deprivation
points.detail: Affective, behavioural and cognitive consequences of insufficient sleep, and the distinction between partial and total sleep deprivation.

questions.q: Describe one affective, one behavioural and one cognitive effect of partial sleep deprivation.
answer: Affective: increased irritability, mood swings and reduced ability to regulate emotional responses.
Behavioural: clumsiness, slowed reaction time and increased risk taking.
Cognitive: reduced concentration, impaired decision making and difficulty encoding new information into memory.

points.title: Sleep deprivation and blood alcohol concentration
points.detail: The comparison of the effects of 17 and 24 hours of sleep deprivation with blood alcohol concentrations of 0.05 and 0.10 on cognitive and motor performance.

questions.q: Explain the comparison drawn between sleep deprivation and blood alcohol concentration, and state one limitation of the comparison.
answer: Seventeen hours without sleep produces impairment in concentration, reaction time and hand-eye coordination comparable with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05.
Twenty-four hours without sleep produces impairment comparable with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10.
A limitation is that the comparison applies only to cognitive and motor performance, and the affective and physiological effects of the two states are not equivalent.

points.title: Circadian rhythm sleep disorders
points.detail: Delayed sleep phase syndrome, advanced sleep phase disorder and shift work sleep disorder, and the mismatch between the internal rhythm and external demands.

questions.q: Describe delayed sleep phase syndrome and explain why it is classified as a circadian rhythm sleep disorder.
answer: A person with delayed sleep phase syndrome consistently falls asleep and wakes several hours later than conventional times, most commonly in adolescence.
Sleep itself is normal in quality and duration when the person is allowed to follow their own schedule.
It is a circadian rhythm disorder because the problem is a persistent misalignment between the internal sleep-wake cycle and the socially required schedule, not a problem with sleep itself.

points.title: Bright light therapy and sleep hygiene
points.detail: Using timed bright light exposure to shift the circadian rhythm, and the sleep hygiene practices that support consistent, high-quality sleep.

questions.q: Explain how bright light therapy is used to treat delayed sleep phase syndrome and name two sleep hygiene practices that support it.
answer: The person is exposed to bright light soon after their desired waking time, which suppresses melatonin and advances the circadian rhythm earlier.
Over consecutive days the sleep onset time shifts earlier to align with the required schedule.
Supporting sleep hygiene practices include keeping a consistent bedtime and wake time, and avoiding screens, caffeine and vigorous exercise in the hours before bed.

points.title: The mental wellbeing continuum
points.detail: Mentally healthy, mental health problem and mental disorder as positions on a continuum; the fluid movement along it and the factors that influence position.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the mental wellbeing continuum and why a person's position on it can change.
answer: The continuum ranges from mentally healthy, through experiencing a mental health problem, to having a diagnosed mental disorder.
A person's position is fluid and can move in either direction over time rather than being fixed.
Position is influenced by the balance of stressors and protective factors, such as the onset of a significant stressor or the strengthening of social support.

points.title: Levels of functioning, resilience and social wellbeing
points.detail: The criteria used to assess mental wellbeing: level of functioning, resilience and social and emotional wellbeing, and what each indicates.

questions.q: Define resilience and level of functioning, and explain how each is used to assess mental wellbeing.
answer: Level of functioning is the degree to which a person can carry out the everyday tasks of independent living, work or study, and relationships.
Resilience is the ability to adapt to and recover from adversity and to restore positive functioning.
High functioning and high resilience indicate a position towards the mentally healthy end of the continuum, while a decline in either suggests movement towards a mental health problem.

points.title: Social and emotional wellbeing framework
points.detail: The Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander view of wellbeing as a multidimensional and holistic concept encompassing connection to body, mind and emotions, family, community, culture, Country and spirituality.

questions.q: Describe the social and emotional wellbeing framework and explain how it differs from a purely individual model of mental health.
answer: Wellbeing is understood holistically as connection to body and behaviours, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, Country and spirituality and ancestors.
These domains are interconnected, so a disruption to one, such as disconnection from Country, affects overall wellbeing.
It differs from an individual model by locating wellbeing in relationships, collective identity and history rather than solely in the individual's internal state.

points.title: Stress, anxiety and phobia
points.detail: Distinguishing stress as a response to a stressor, anxiety as apprehension about a future threat, and phobia as a persistent, excessive fear that causes significant distress and avoidance.

questions.q: Distinguish between anxiety and a specific phobia, and state what makes a phobia a diagnosable disorder.
answer: Anxiety is a feeling of apprehension or uneasiness about an anticipated event and is a normal, adaptive response experienced by everyone.
A specific phobia is a persistent, intense and irrational fear of a particular object or situation that is out of proportion to any actual danger.
It is diagnosable because it causes significant distress and avoidance behaviour that impairs the person's everyday functioning, typically persisting for six months or more.

points.title: Biological contributors to specific phobia
points.detail: GABA dysfunction, long-term potentiation of fear associations, and the role of the stress response in maintaining a phobia.

questions.q: Explain how GABA dysfunction and long-term potentiation contribute to the development of a specific phobia.
answer: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter, so insufficient GABA production or reception leaves the nervous system under-inhibited and over-aroused.
This heightened arousal makes an intense fear response more likely and more difficult to calm.
Long-term potentiation strengthens the neural pathway linking the phobic stimulus to the fear response each time it is activated, so the association becomes more readily and more strongly triggered.

points.title: Psychological contributors to specific phobia
points.detail: Precipitation by classical conditioning and perpetuation by operant conditioning, together with cognitive bias including memory bias and catastrophic thinking.

questions.q: Explain how classical and operant conditioning together precipitate and perpetuate a specific phobia of dogs.
answer: Classical conditioning precipitates the phobia: a previously neutral stimulus, the dog, is paired with a frightening event such as being bitten, so the dog becomes a conditioned stimulus producing a fear response.
Operant conditioning perpetuates the phobia: the person avoids dogs, which removes the unpleasant feeling of fear.
This is negative reinforcement, so avoidance behaviour is strengthened and repeated.
Because the person never encounters a dog without harm, the fear association is never extinguished.

points.title: Cognitive bias in specific phobia
points.detail: Memory bias as the distorted recall of information consistent with the fear, and catastrophic thinking as the overestimation of the likelihood and severity of a feared outcome.

questions.q: Define catastrophic thinking and memory bias, and give an example of each for a person with a phobia of flying.
answer: Catastrophic thinking is a cognitive bias in which the person overestimates the likelihood and severity of the worst possible outcome, such as being certain that turbulence means the plane will crash.
Memory bias is a distortion in what is recalled so that information consistent with the fear is remembered more readily.
For example, the person vividly recalls news reports of crashes but not the far greater number of safe flights.

points.title: Social contributors to specific phobia
points.detail: Specific environmental triggers and the role of stigma around seeking treatment in maintaining a phobia.

questions.q: Explain how stigma can act as a social factor that perpetuates a specific phobia.
answer: Stigma involves negative attitudes and beliefs held in the community about mental health conditions or about seeking help.
A person who fears being judged as weak or irrational may conceal the phobia and delay or avoid treatment.
Without evidence-based intervention the avoidance behaviour continues to be reinforced, so the phobia persists or worsens.

points.title: Biopsychosocial interventions for specific phobia
points.detail: Short-acting anti-anxiety benzodiazepine agents and breathing retraining; cognitive behavioural therapy and systematic desensitisation; psychoeducation for families and supporters.

questions.q: Describe systematic desensitisation and explain why it is classified as a psychological intervention.
answer: The person is taught a relaxation technique such as progressive muscle relaxation or controlled breathing.
A fear hierarchy is constructed, ranking exposures to the phobic stimulus from least to most anxiety-provoking.
The person works up the hierarchy while remaining relaxed, so the phobic stimulus is progressively paired with relaxation rather than fear.
It is a psychological intervention because it targets the learned association through counterconditioning rather than altering biology or the social environment.

points.title: Benzodiazepines and breathing retraining
points.detail: The action of GABA agonists in enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission, and the role of breathing retraining in reducing hyperventilation and physiological arousal.

questions.q: Explain how a short-acting benzodiazepine reduces anxiety, and state one reason it is not a long-term solution.
answer: Benzodiazepines act as GABA agonists, mimicking or enhancing the effect of GABA at the postsynaptic receptor.
This increases inhibitory neurotransmission, reducing neural excitation and therefore the physiological symptoms of anxiety.
They treat only the symptoms and not the learned fear association, and prolonged use carries a risk of dependence and tolerance.

points.title: Cognitive behavioural therapy and psychoeducation
points.detail: Identifying and challenging unhelpful thoughts and replacing them with adaptive behaviours; educating families and supporters to avoid reinforcing avoidance.

questions.q: Explain the purpose of psychoeducation for the family of a person with a specific phobia.
answer: Psychoeducation teaches the family about the nature of the phobia and the evidence-based treatments available.
Families learn not to reinforce avoidance behaviours, for example by not completing the feared task on the person's behalf.
They are also taught to encourage engagement with and adherence to treatment, which improves outcomes.

points.title: Protective factors for mental wellbeing
points.detail: Adequate sleep, a balanced diet and hydration, and cognitive behavioural strategies and mindfulness meditation as protective factors, alongside cultural determinants.

questions.q: Explain how two protective factors support mental wellbeing, naming one biological and one psychological factor.
answer: Biological: adequate sleep allows neural repair and consolidation and supports emotional regulation, so the person is better able to cope with stressors.
Psychological: mindfulness meditation directs attention to the present moment without judgement, reducing rumination and physiological arousal.
Both raise the threshold at which a stressor produces a mental health problem, supporting resilience.

points.title: Cultural determinants as protective factors
points.detail: Cultural continuity and self-determination as protective factors for the social and emotional wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

questions.q: Explain how cultural continuity and self-determination act as protective factors for social and emotional wellbeing.
answer: Cultural continuity is the passing on of knowledge, language, practices and connection to Country across generations, which strengthens identity and belonging.
Self-determination is the right of communities to make decisions about matters affecting them, including the design and delivery of health services.
Both restore control and connection that were disrupted by colonisation, and communities with higher levels of each show better wellbeing outcomes.

points.title: Designing the investigation
points.detail: Developing a question and hypothesis, selecting a methodology and design, identifying variables and controls, and planning for ethical compliance.

questions.q: State three decisions that must be documented when planning a psychological investigation and why each matters.
answer: The research design, because a within or between subjects choice determines which extraneous variables must be managed.
The sampling and allocation technique, because it determines how far the results can be generalised.
The ethical procedures, including consent, confidentiality and debriefing, because the investigation cannot proceed without them.

points.title: Collecting and processing data
points.detail: Quantitative and qualitative, objective and subjective data; recording data in tables and calculating measures of central tendency and spread.

questions.q: Distinguish between objective and subjective data and give an example of each in a study of sleep.
answer: Objective data are observable and measurable independently of the participant's interpretation, such as EEG recordings of brain wave frequency.
Subjective data depend on the participant's own report or the researcher's judgement, such as a self-rated sleep quality score in a sleep diary.
Both are useful, but subjective data are more vulnerable to bias, so studies often collect them alongside objective measures.

points.title: Analysing and evaluating
points.detail: Interpreting patterns in results, evaluating the reliability and validity of the method, identifying uncontrolled variables and stating the limits on generalisation.

questions.q: Explain the difference between reliability and validity in a psychological investigation and give an example of a study that is reliable but not valid.
answer: Reliability is the consistency of results if the study is repeated under the same conditions.
Validity is whether the study measures what it claims to measure and whether the conclusion drawn is justified.
A questionnaire that produces the same score every time but actually measures general mood rather than the intended anxiety construct is reliable but not valid.

points.title: Communicating findings
points.detail: The structure of a scientific report or poster, referencing conventions, and the requirement to report findings honestly including results that do not support the hypothesis.

questions.q: State what a conclusion in a psychological report must include and one thing it must not claim.
answer: It must state whether the results supported the hypothesis, referring to the specific data such as the group means.
It must be limited to the population sampled and the variables as operationalised.
It must not claim that the hypothesis has been proven, since a single study provides evidence rather than proof.
